newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: TAP axes four more flights, pilots mull work order.
newsitem.headline: TAP axes four more flights, pilots mull work order.

text.p: TAP-Air Portugal cancelled four more flights on Sunday, despite a government decree ordering pilots back to work after they voted overwhelmingly in favour of more strikes against working hours.
The cancellations came as the airline waited to see if pilots would comply with the government order after warning them that their actions could result in a nosedive in the carrier's profits.
Failure to comply with the government order could land offending pilots in jail for up to five years.
Pilots who cancelled flights to Hamburg, Berlin and Geneva said they were ill or had trade union duties, said airline spokesman Raul Alves Fernandes.
TAP was seeking an explanation from one pilot who gave no reason for cancelling his flight to Barcelona, he said.
Stranded passengers were re-routed to their destinations on other flights.

After an extraordinary cabinet meeting on Saturday afternoon, the socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres issued a special decree ordering pilots back to work to protect the public interest and safeguard jobs at the airline.

TAP pilots had gone back on strike on Saturday, forcing the cancellation of three flights that day. The pilots had decided on Thursday night to resume an indefinite strike, and were refusing to operate flights laid on at short notice.
They said the strike, which has been on and off for more than two weeks, was a protest against the chaotic organisation of working hours.

The government says it is doing all it can to satisfy the pilots' demands by pressing ahead with plans to invest 800 million escudos ($4.2 million) to upgrade the computer system which works out flight and work schedules.

Officials at the Civil Aviation Pilots' Union (SPAC), which represents all of TAP's 430 pilots, said they were consulting lawyers to verify that the government's decision to order them back to work was legal.
"SPAC will attack the government's decision if it is found to be illegal," one unidentified SPAC official told the Portuguese news agency Lusa on Saturday night.
"We regret that the government, which claims to be democratic, had to resort to force and coercion to resolve a labour dispute," the official added.
Government officials had warned that the strikes during the peak summer holiday season could point TAP towards bankruptcy.
In April, TAP forecast that it could turn a profit in 1997, a first for more than two decades. Estimates of the cost of the dispute were not immediately available.
The pilots began their protest two weekends ago, forcing TAP to cancel 12 flights and stranding at least 1,300 people.
The pilots then suspended the strike until Friday night to continue talks with management and government officials. After the talks failed, they voted overwhelmingly to resume the strike.
Last April TAP's pilots staged a two-day strike in a separate protest over working hours, grounding international flights and stranding 14,000 passengers.
